lessons.title: Study Session 1: Giving an AI Tool Worked Examples Inside a Prompt

blocks.text: Introduction Custódio Machava processes incoming claims at an insurance office in Xai-Xai, and had spent weeks instructing an AI tool, in plain sentences, on exactly how to categorise each claim description, only to keep receiving three or four subtly different category labels for what were, in every practical sense, the same kind of claim. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about a model's ability to learn a task from examples shown directly in a prompt. Distinguish a prompt containing worked examples from one relying on instructions alone. Apply a method for selecting examples that actually demonstrate the pattern a task requires. Recognise when added examples are making a prompt's output less consistent rather than more. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Three Labels for the Same Kind of Claim Custódio Machava's insurance office in Xai-Xai needed incoming claims sorted into a fixed set of categories before they reached an adjuster, and Custódio had written increasingly detailed plain-language instructions telling an AI tool exactly how each category should be defined. Despite the detail, claims that were, in every practical sense, describing the same kind of incident kept coming back labelled three or four different ways, as though the written instructions alone were never quite specific enough to pin the categories down. 2.2 What Research Found About Learning From Examples in a Prompt In 2020, a large research team led by Tom Brown published a study at the Neural Information Processing Systems conference examining a large language model's ability to perform a new task after seeing only a handful of worked examples placed directly inside its prompt, with no further training involved. Their finding was that performance improved substantially once a few demonstrated examples were included alongside an instruction, compared to giving the same model only the instruction on its own. 2.3 Choosing Examples That Actually Demonstrate a Pattern Picking Examples That Cover the Genuinely Confusing Cases Selecting worked examples specifically from the cases that have caused inconsistent output in the past, rather than only the clearest, easiest cases, is what actually teaches a model the distinction an instruction alone struggled to convey. Keeping Examples Consistent With Each Other Checking that every worked example included in a prompt follows the exact same format and logic as the others prevents the examples themselves from introducing a second, competing source of inconsistency. 2.4 Key Practices Select worked examples from cases that have previously caused inconsistent categorisation. Keep every example in a prompt consistent with the others in format and logic. Limit examples to a handful that clearly demonstrate the pattern, rather than an exhaustive list. Test a new example-based prompt against the exact cases that originally caused confusion. 2.5 A Worked Example: Custódio's Example-Based Prompt Custódio pulled the five claims that had most often been categorised inconsistently and built a prompt around them as worked examples, showing the claim description alongside its correct category for each one, before asking the AI tool to categorise a new batch. The new batch, including several claims similar in wording to the earlier troublesome ones, came back with a single consistent category applied to each genuinely similar case. The insurance office's categorisation backlog cleared noticeably faster once adjusters no longer had to manually reconcile conflicting labels for the same kind of claim. The written instructions Custódio had spent weeks refining had never been unclear to a human reader. They had simply never shown the model what a correctly categorised claim actually looked like, and only the worked examples ever closed that particular gap. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Relying entirely on detailed written instructions, without ever showing a model a worked example of the actual task performed correctly, can leave a prompt producing inconsistent output even when the instructions themselves read perfectly clearly to a human. Choosing only the easiest, clearest examples for a prompt, while skipping the genuinely confusing cases, fails to teach a model the specific distinction it actually needs. 2.7 A Clear Instruction and a Clear Example Are Not the Same Thing Custódio's original written instructions had described the claim categories accurately and in careful detail. That accuracy on its own was not what closed the gap. Only a handful of actual worked examples ever gave the AI tool something concrete to match new claims against. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to select worked examples that demonstrate a task's genuinely confusing cases, rather than relying on instructions alone. Study Session 2 turns from showing a model examples to structuring a prompt so it works through a problem in explicit reasoning steps.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a task where an AI tool's output has been inconsistent despite clear instructions. Have you tried showing it worked examples instead? 2. Build a prompt with three to five worked examples drawn from a real task's genuinely confusing cases, and test it against those cases. Practical Output: Practical Output An example-based prompt for one real categorisation or classification task, built from worked examples drawn from previously inconsistent cases. 7.0 References and Further Reading Brown, T.B., Mann, B., Ryder, N., et al. (2020). Language models are few-shot learners. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020). Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: 1 Corinthians 10:11, on things happening as examples, written for admonition. Qur'an, Surah Yusuf 12:111, on there being a lesson in their stories for those of understanding.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Breaking a Task Into Explicit Reasoning Steps

blocks.text: Introduction Voahangy Razafindrakoto lost her husband four years ago and has run the household on her own since, alongside analysing budget variances for a district finance office in Toamasina, where she found that asking an AI tool directly for a final variance explanation produced confident answers that, on closer inspection, had skipped over which specific line items actually drove the change. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about prompting a model to show intermediate reasoning steps. Distinguish a prompt that asks for step-by-step reasoning from one that asks only for a final answer. Apply a method for structuring a prompt so a model works through a problem in explicit stages. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Confident Answer With No Visible Working Voahangy Razafindrakoto's district finance office in Toamasina needed monthly budget variances explained clearly enough for a committee to act on, and Voahangy had been asking an AI tool directly for a final explanation of each variance. The answers read confidently and plausibly, but a colleague checking one against the underlying figures found the explanation had skipped past the two specific line items actually responsible for the change, naming a general cause instead. 2.2 What Research Found About Prompting for Reasoning Steps In 2022, the researcher Jason Wei and colleagues published a study at the Neural Information Processing Systems conference examining what happened when a large language model was prompted to produce its intermediate reasoning before stating a final answer. Their finding was that prompting for this chain of reasoning steps substantially improved performance on tasks involving arithmetic, logic and multi-step calculation, compared to prompts that asked only for a direct final answer. 2.3 Structuring a Prompt for Explicit Stages Asking for the Working, Not Only the Conclusion Explicitly instructing a prompt to identify each contributing figure, calculate its individual effect, and only then state a conclusion, forces a model to surface the specific reasoning a final-answer-only request tends to skip past. Checking Each Reasoning Step Against the Underlying Figures Reviewing each intermediate step a model produces against the actual source data, rather than only checking whether the final conclusion sounds reasonable, is what actually catches a step that quietly skipped over a relevant figure. 2.4 Key Practices Instruct a prompt to identify contributing figures and calculate their effect before stating a conclusion. Review each intermediate reasoning step against the underlying source data. Ask specifically which line items or figures a variance explanation is actually built on. Treat a plausible-sounding final answer with no visible working as incomplete, not finished. 2.5 A Worked Example: Voahangy's Step-by-Step Prompt For the following month's variance report, Voahangy restructured her prompt to instruct the AI tool to list every line item showing meaningful change, calculate each one's individual contribution to the total variance, and only then summarise the overall cause. The resulting explanation named the same two line items the colleague's manual check had found the previous month, this time surfaced directly by the model's own visible reasoning. The finance committee's questions that month focused specifically on the two named line items, a level of detail the earlier general explanations had never actually supported. The AI tool's earlier direct answers had never been fabricated. They had simply skipped the working that would have let anyone check where the conclusion actually came from, and only asking for that working explicitly ever made it visible. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Asking an AI tool directly for a final variance explanation, without instructing it to show which specific figures the explanation is built on, risks producing a plausible-sounding answer that has quietly skipped over the actual contributing detail, exactly what happened with Voahangy's earlier reports. Checking only whether a final answer sounds reasonable, rather than verifying each reasoning step against real data, lets this kind of skipped detail pass unnoticed. 2.7 Plausible Is Not the Same as Shown Every one of the AI tool's earlier direct variance explanations had sounded entirely plausible to anyone reading it. Sounding plausible had never meant the explanation could actually be traced back to specific figures, and only asking the model to show that trail explicitly ever made the difference visible. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to prompt a model for explicit reasoning steps rather than a direct final answer alone. Study Session 3 turns from structuring reasoning to testing whether assigning a role or persona to an AI tool genuinely improves its output at all.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a recent AI-generated explanation you accepted. Could you actually trace it back to specific supporting figures, or did it simply sound reasonable? 2. Restructure one real prompt to require explicit reasoning steps before a final answer, and check each step against real data. Practical Output: Practical Output A step-by-step reasoning prompt for one real calculation or analysis task, showing each intermediate step checked against underlying source data. 7.0 References and Further Reading Wei, J., Wang, X., Schuurmans, D., et al. (2022). Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022), 24824 to 24837. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Isaiah 1:18, on coming and reasoning together. Qur'an, Surah Al-Ankabut 29:43, on examples understood only by those of knowledge.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Assigning a Role Without Assuming It Automatically Helps

blocks.text: Introduction Thabo Ramaili writes outreach messages for a trades apprenticeship centre in Teyateyaneng, and had spent months opening every prompt by telling the AI tool it was an experienced marketing director, a habit picked up early on and never once actually tested against a prompt without that instruction. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about assigning a persona or role in a system prompt. Distinguish a role assignment tested for actual effect from one assumed to help by default. Apply a method for checking whether a role assignment is genuinely improving a specific task's output. Recognise when a role assignment is being kept out of habit rather than demonstrated benefit. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Habit Never Actually Tested Thabo Ramaili writes outreach messages for a trades apprenticeship centre in Teyateyaneng, and had picked up the habit, early on, of opening every prompt with an instruction telling the AI tool it was an experienced marketing director before asking for a draft. The habit had simply carried on for months, repeated automatically at the start of every prompt, without Thabo ever actually comparing what the tool produced with and without that opening line. 2.2 What Research Found About Persona Assignment in Prompts In 2024, the researchers Mingqian Zheng, Jiaxin Pei, Lajanugen Logeswaran, Moontae Lee and David Jurgens tested 162 assigned roles against four popular language model families across 2,410 factual questions, publishing their results in the Findings track of EMNLP 2024. Their finding was that adding a persona to a system prompt did not improve performance compared to no persona at all, with only small, inconsistent gains appearing for certain specific role types. 2.3 Checking Whether a Role Assignment Actually Helps Comparing Output With and Without the Role Assignment Running the same task twice, once with a role assignment included and once without it, and comparing the two outputs directly against the actual requirements of the task is what reveals whether the assignment is doing anything measurable at all. Dropping a Role Assignment That Shows No Measurable Difference Removing a role assignment once a direct comparison shows no meaningful difference in output keeps a prompt only as long and complicated as it actually needs to be. 2.4 Key Practices Run a task with and without a role assignment before assuming the assignment helps. Compare the two outputs directly against the task's actual requirements, not general impressions. Drop a role assignment that shows no measurable difference in a direct comparison. Retest a role assignment periodically, since a genuine benefit for one task may not hold for another. Keep a short record of which role assignments have actually been tested and confirmed useful. 2.5 A Worked Example: Thabo's Side-by-Side Comparison Thabo ran the same outreach message request twice, once with the marketing director role assignment and once without it, and placed the two drafts side by side for a colleague to review without knowing which was which. The colleague could not reliably tell the two apart, and neither draft was judged noticeably stronger than the other on tone, clarity or persuasiveness. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Carrying a role assignment forward simply because it was used once early on, without ever comparing output with and without it, allows a habit to sit in every prompt indefinitely regardless of whether it is doing anything measurable, which is exactly what had happened with Thabo's marketing director instruction. Assuming a role assignment must help because it feels like a reasonable, professional-sounding addition overlooks the specific finding that persona assignment often shows no real effect. 2.7 A Habit Repeated Is Not the Same as a Technique Confirmed The marketing director instruction in Thabo's prompts had never caused any obvious harm to the outreach messages it produced. No direct comparison had ever put it to the test, and only actually running it side by side against a version without it ever revealed what it was and was not doing. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to test a role assignment directly rather than assuming it helps by default. Study Session 4 turns from testing individual prompt elements to building a reusable template for a task performed repeatedly.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a role or persona instruction you use in your own prompts. Have you ever tested it directly against a version without it? 2. Run one real prompt twice, with and without a role assignment, and compare the two outputs against the task's actual requirements. Practical Output: Practical Output A side-by-side comparison of one real prompt run with and without a role assignment, with a judgment on whether the assignment showed a measurable difference. 7.0 References and Further Reading Zheng, M., Pei, J., Logeswaran, L., Lee, M., & Jurgens, D. (2024). When "a helpful assistant" is not really helpful: Personas in system prompts do not improve performances of large language models. Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Matthew 7:16, on knowing them by their fruits. Qur'an, Surah Muhammad 47:31, on being tested until what is genuine is made evident.

options: The insurance office's claim categories were poorly defined
Detailed instructions alone can leave a prompt inconsistent without a worked example demonstrating the actual task
Insurance offices should not use AI tools for categorisation
Custódio had written the instructions in the wrong language

options: Providing longer written instructions with no examples
Including a handful of worked examples directly in the prompt, without further training
Reducing the number of instructions given to the model
Repeating the same instruction multiple times in a row
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Giving an AI Tool Worked Examples Inside a Prompt) before continuing.

options: Only the clearest, easiest cases available
Cases that have previously caused inconsistent output
A single example, regardless of the task's complexity
Cases chosen entirely at random

quiz.q: An AI tool's direct variance explanation had skipped the two line items that actually drove the change. What did this reveal?
options: The underlying budget data had been recorded incorrectly
A prompt asking only for a final answer can skip the specific reasoning that would let the answer be checked
District finance offices should not use AI tools for variance analysis
The finance committee had misread the explanation
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Breaking a Task Into Explicit Reasoning Steps) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Wei and colleagues' 2022 research, what improved a model's performance on multi-step tasks?
options: Asking only for a direct final answer
Prompting the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps before a final answer
Removing all instructions from the prompt
Repeating the same final answer request several times

quiz.q: What does this session recommend instructing a prompt to do before stating a conclusion?
options: Nothing further; a conclusion should be stated immediately
Identify contributing figures and calculate their individual effect
Skip directly to the most likely explanation
Avoid referencing any specific figures at all

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Building a Reusable Prompt Template for a Repeated Task

blocks.text: Introduction Ilda Sumbo coordinates hiring at a manufacturing company in Benguela, and had been writing a completely new prompt from scratch every time a job description needed drafting, spending nearly as long rebuilding the request as she once spent writing the description by hand. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about cataloguing reusable prompt patterns. Distinguish a reusable prompt template from a one-off prompt written fresh each time. Apply a method for turning a working prompt into a template that can be reused for similar future tasks. Recognise when a template has stopped matching the task it was originally built for. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Rebuilding the Same Request From Scratch, Every Time Ilda Sumbo coordinates hiring at a manufacturing company in Benguela, and each time a new job description needed drafting, she wrote an entirely new prompt from the ground up, choosing the structure, tone instructions and formatting fresh every time. A colleague pointed out that Ilda was spending nearly as long rebuilding the request itself as she had once spent writing job descriptions directly by hand, with no benefit carried over from one prompt to the next. 2.2 What Research Found About Cataloguing Reusable Prompt Patterns In 2023, the researchers Jules White, Quchen Fu, Sam Hays and colleagues published a preprint organising recurring prompt engineering solutions into a named catalog of patterns, each addressing a specific, repeatable structural need. Their finding was that effective prompt structures could be catalogued and reused across many different tasks, rather than being reinvented individually every time a similar problem arose. 2.3 Turning a Working Prompt Into a Template Separating the Fixed Structure From the Task-Specific Detail Identifying exactly which parts of a successful prompt stay the same across similar tasks, and which parts change with each specific job, turns a one-off prompt into a template with clearly marked places to fill in new detail. Naming and Storing a Template for Future Reuse Giving a working template a clear name and keeping it somewhere easy to find, rather than leaving it buried in a single past conversation, is what actually makes it reusable the next time the same kind of task comes up. 2.4 Key Practices Identify which parts of a successful prompt stay fixed across similar tasks and which vary. Mark the variable parts of a template clearly, so new detail can be filled in without rebuilding the structure. Name and store a working template somewhere easy to find and reuse. Set a reminder to check, every few months, whether a template's structure still fits the task. 2.5 A Worked Example: Ilda's Job Description Template After the colleague's observation, Ilda took her most successful recent job description prompt and separated it into a fixed structure, role title, key responsibilities, required qualifications, tone, with clearly marked blanks for whatever changed from one posting to the next. The following month's five new job descriptions were each drafted by filling in the template's blanks, cutting the time spent on prompt-writing to a fraction of what it had taken before. Ilda's earlier practice of rebuilding a prompt from scratch each time had never produced a bad job description. It had simply thrown away, every single time, the structure that had already worked the time before, and only separating that structure from the task-specific detail ever let it actually be reused. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Writing a completely new prompt from scratch for a task that recurs regularly discards a working structure that could otherwise have been reused, the exact habit that had Ilda spending nearly as much time on the prompt as on the job description itself. Leaving a successful prompt buried in a single past conversation, rather than naming and storing it as a template, makes it just as hard to find and reuse as never having written it at all. 2.7 A Working Prompt Only Helps Once Unless It Is Saved Every prompt Ilda had written before building her template had, on its own, worked well enough to produce a usable job description. None of that success had carried forward to the next posting, and only turning one working prompt into a reusable template ever let its usefulness extend beyond the single task it was first written for. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to separate a working prompt's fixed structure from its task-specific detail and store it as a reusable template. Study Session 5 turns from building a template to testing whether it actually stays stable under small variations.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a task you prompt an AI tool for repeatedly. Do you rebuild the prompt each time, or reuse a saved template? 2. Turn one real successful prompt into a template, separating its fixed structure from clearly marked task-specific blanks. Practical Output: Practical Output A reusable prompt template for one real repeated task, with its fixed structure separated from clearly marked variable detail. 7.0 References and Further Reading White, J., Fu, Q., Hays, S., et al. (2023). A prompt pattern catalog to enhance prompt engineering with ChatGPT. arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.11382. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Titus 2:7, on showing oneself a pattern of good works. Qur'an, Surah Al-Mumtahanah 60:4, on there having been an excellent pattern in Abraham.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Testing a Prompt for Small Changes That Break It

blocks.text: Introduction Emmanuel Nshimiyimana fled the Democratic Republic of the Congo as a boy and today reviews eligibility files for displaced families at a support office in Rubavu, where a template he had built for summarising those files worked perfectly the first three times he used it, then produced a completely different, unusable structure the fourth time, after nothing more than a single word in the file had changed. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about a prompt's sensitivity to small wording changes. Distinguish a prompt tested for stability from one trusted after a single successful try. Apply a method for testing a prompt template against small variations before relying on it repeatedly. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 The Same Template, Broken by One Different Word Emmanuel uses a saved prompt template to summarise eligibility files at his office in Rubavu, and the template had produced a clean, consistent summary the first three times he tried it. On the fourth file, where the only meaningful difference was a single word describing the applicant's household situation, the same template produced a summary in a completely different structure, missing a section the earlier three had all reliably included. 2.2 What Research Found About Prompt Sensitivity In 2024, the researchers Abel Salinas and Fred Morstatter published a study examining how large language models responded to small alterations in prompt wording, punctuation and formatting, appearing in the Findings track of the Association for Computational Linguistics' 2024 conference. Their finding was that minor changes, ones that left the underlying task genuinely unchanged, could substantially shift a model's output or flip a decision entirely, a pattern they described as a butterfly effect running through prompt-based systems. 2.3 Testing a Template Against Small Variations Deliberately Varying Wording That Should Not Matter Running a template several times with small, deliberate changes, a different word choice, a reordered sentence, an extra space, checks whether the template's output stays stable across variations that should have no real bearing on the task. Treating Early Success as a Starting Point, Not Proof of Stability Recognising that a template working correctly the first few times says nothing about how it will handle the next input, and testing it against a wider range of realistic variations before relying on it repeatedly, is what actually establishes whether it is stable. 2.4 Key Practices Run a new template several times with small, deliberate wording variations before trusting it. Test a template against realistic edge cases, not only the cleanest example inputs. Treat a template's early successes as a starting point, not confirmation of long-term stability. Log any input that produces an unexpectedly different output, and adjust the template accordingly. 2.5 A Worked Example: Emmanuel's Variation Test After the fourth file broke the template, Emmanuel deliberately ran it against ten further files chosen specifically for small wording differences from one another, rather than picking the cleanest ten available. Two more files produced a structure that dropped the same section the fourth file had, revealing a specific wording pattern the template consistently struggled with rather than a one-off fluke. Emmanuel adjusted the template to explicitly instruct the AI tool to always include that section regardless of how a household situation was described, and a further round of variation testing produced consistent summaries across every file tried. The template's first three smooth successes had never been a false signal exactly. No one had yet tried it against the kind of small variation that turned out to matter, and only deliberately seeking that variation out ever revealed the gap. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Trusting a new prompt template after only a few smooth, successful early uses, without deliberately testing it against small realistic variations, leaves a template vulnerable to breaking on exactly the kind of input that had not yet been tried, which is what happened when a single changed word derailed Emmanuel's fourth file. Testing a template only against clean, easy example inputs, rather than realistic edge cases, hides instability that only shows up once messier real-world input arrives. 2.7 Working Three Times Is Not the Same as Working Reliably Emmanuel's template had genuinely worked, without any flaw, on each of its first three uses. Three clean successes counted for less than they seemed to, and only deliberately testing the template against small, realistic changes ever showed where it actually broke. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to test a prompt template against small, deliberate variations before trusting it for repeated use. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning to how a prompt is designed and revised through a structured, ongoing process rather than ad hoc tinkering.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a prompt template you have relied on after only a few successful uses. Have you tested it against small realistic variations? 2. Test one real prompt template against at least five small, deliberate wording variations and note any input that breaks it. Practical Output: Practical Output A variation-testing log for one real prompt template, showing at least five tested wording variations and any output that broke or diverged. 7.0 References and Further Reading Salinas, A., & Morstatter, F. (2024). The butterfly effect of altering prompts: How small changes and jailbreaks affect large language model performance. Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2024. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Psalm 26:2, on being examined, proved and tried. Qur'an, Surah Al-Anbya 21:35, on being tested with trial.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Running a Structured Process to Design and Refine a Prompt

blocks.text: Introduction Espérance Nduwimana turns field data into narrative summaries for a development NGO in Gitega, and had been revising a stubborn prompt for months through what amounted to random tinkering, changing a word here, adding a sentence there, with no way to explain afterward why any particular change had actually helped. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about how non-expert prompt writers actually approach designing a prompt. Distinguish a structured, iterative approach to prompt design from an unsystematic trial-and-error one. Apply a method for revising a prompt through a deliberate, repeatable process rather than ad hoc tinkering. Recognise when a prompt-design process has stalled without a clear next step. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Months of Tinkering, No Clear Record of What Helped Espérance Nduwimana turns raw field data into narrative summaries for a development NGO in Gitega, and a particular summary prompt had proven stubbornly inconsistent for months. Espérance had been revising it by changing a word here, adding a sentence there, whenever a summary came out wrong, but had no actual record of which specific changes had helped and which had simply coincided with a better outcome by chance. 2.2 What Research Found About Non-Expert Prompt Design In 2023, the researchers J.D. Zamfirescu-Pereira, Richmond Wong, Bjoern Hartmann and Qian Yang observed how non-expert prompt designers actually approached the task, publishing their findings at that year's premier human-computer interaction conference, CHI. Their finding was that these designers tended to write single prompts optimistically rather than systematically iterating, drew broad conclusions from very small numbers of examples, and lacked any structured process for revising a prompt once it had failed. 2.3 Building a Repeatable Revision Process Changing One Element at a Time and Recording the Result Revising a prompt one specific element at a time, testing the change against a consistent set of inputs, and recording whether it actually improved the output is what turns tinkering into a process someone could explain and repeat afterward. Setting a Clear Stopping Point Before Starting a Revision Deciding, before beginning a round of revision, what specific improvement would count as success is what keeps a revision process from continuing indefinitely without any way to tell whether it has actually stalled. 2.4 Key Practices Change one specific prompt element at a time, rather than several elements at once. Test each change against a consistent set of inputs before deciding whether it helped. Record which specific changes improved output and which did not. Decide, before a revision round begins, what would count as a successful improvement. 2.5 A Worked Example: Espérance's Structured Revision Log Espérance began keeping a simple log, testing one change to the summary prompt at a time against the same five sample field reports, and recording each attempt's outcome before moving to the next change. The third recorded change, restructuring how the prompt asked for regional context to be summarised, was the one that actually resolved the inconsistency, a result the earlier months of unrecorded tinkering had never actually isolated. Espérance could, for the first time, explain exactly which change had fixed the summary prompt and why, a clarity the previous months of scattered adjustments had never produced despite plenty of individual effort. None of Espérance's earlier changes had necessarily been wrong choices. They had simply been made without any way to track which ones actually mattered, and only a structured, one-change-at-a-time log ever made that visible. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Changing several elements of a prompt at once, whenever an output looks wrong, makes it impossible to know afterward which specific change actually caused an improvement, exactly the position Espérance's unrecorded months of tinkering had ended up in. Revising a prompt indefinitely without deciding beforehand what would count as success leaves a process with no way to recognise when it has actually stalled rather than simply needing one more small adjustment. 2.7 Effort Without a Record Is Hard to Learn From Espérance's months of prompt tinkering had involved real, careful attention every time a summary came out wrong. What that attention lacked was organisation, some way of showing afterward which specific change had actually mattered, and only a structured log of one change at a time ever turned effort into something worth learning from. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to revise a prompt one element at a time, recording results against a consistent set of inputs. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Prompt Development for Structured Data Tasks, the next course in Pathway 53.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a prompt you have revised repeatedly. Did you change one element at a time and record what helped, or adjust several things at once? 2. Keep a structured revision log for one real prompt, changing one element at a time against a consistent set of test inputs. Practical Output: Practical Output A structured revision log for one real prompt, showing at least three recorded changes tested one at a time against a consistent set of inputs. 7.0 References and Further Reading Zamfirescu-Pereira, J.D., Wong, R., Hartmann, B., & Yang, Q. quiz.q: Ilda was rebuilding a full prompt from scratch for every new job description. What did this reveal?
options: Job descriptions cannot be drafted using AI tools
Writing a fresh prompt each time discards a working structure that could otherwise be reused as a template
Manufacturing companies should not use AI tools for hiring tasks
Ilda's earlier job descriptions had all been inaccurate

quiz.q: According to White and colleagues' 2023 research, what did they find about prompt patterns?
options: Every prompt must be written uniquely for its specific task
Effective prompt structures could be catalogued and reused across many different tasks
Prompt patterns only apply to creative writing tasks
Reusing a prompt structure always produces worse results than writing fresh each time

quiz.q: What does this session recommend identifying when turning a prompt into a template?
options: Nothing; the entire prompt should be rewritten each time regardless
Which parts of the prompt stay fixed across similar tasks and which vary
Only the shortest possible version of the prompt
The single most complicated part of the original prompt

quiz.q: Emmanuel's template broke on its fourth use after only a single word in the file changed. What did this reveal?

A prompt template can be highly sensitive to small wording changes that leave the underlying task unchanged
Resettlement offices should not use AI tools for summarising files
The fourth file had contained inaccurate information

quiz.q: According to Salinas and Morstatter's 2024 research, what did they find about prompt sensitivity?
options: Small wording changes had no meaningful effect on model output
Minor alterations to wording, punctuation or formatting could substantially shift output or flip a decision
Only major changes to a prompt's task could affect model output
Prompt sensitivity only affects models trained on limited data

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing before trusting a new prompt template?
options: Using it once and assuming it will always work the same way
Running it several times with small, deliberate wording variations
Avoiding any testing to save time
Testing it only against the cleanest, easiest example inputs

finalQuiz.q: Custódio's detailed written instructions still produced three or four different labels for the same kind of claim. What did this reveal?
options: The insurance office's claim categories were poorly defined
Detailed instructions alone can leave a prompt inconsistent without a worked example demonstrating the actual task
Insurance offices should not use AI tools for categorisation
Custódio had written the instructions in the wrong language

finalQuiz.q: According to Brown and colleagues' 2020 research, what improved a model's performance on a new task?
options: Providing longer written instructions with no examples
Including a handful of worked examples directly in the prompt, without further training
Reducing the number of instructions given to the model
Repeating the same instruction multiple times in a row
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Giving an AI Tool Worked Examples Inside a Prompt) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend selecting worked examples from?
options: Only the clearest, easiest cases available
Cases that have previously caused inconsistent output
A single example, regardless of the task's complexity
Cases chosen entirely at random

finalQuiz.q: An AI tool's direct variance explanation had skipped the two line items that actually drove the change. What did this reveal?

A prompt asking only for a final answer can skip the specific reasoning that would let the answer be checked

The finance committee had misread the explanation

finalQuiz.q: According to Wei and colleagues' 2022 research, what improved a model's performance on multi-step tasks?
options: Asking only for a direct final answer
Prompting the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps before a final answer
Removing all instructions from the prompt
Repeating the same final answer request several times
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Breaking a Task Into Explicit Reasoning Steps) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend instructing a prompt to do before stating a conclusion?
options: Nothing further; a conclusion should be stated immediately
Identify contributing figures and calculate their individual effect
Skip directly to the most likely explanation
Avoid referencing any specific figures at all
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Breaking a Task Into Explicit Reasoning Steps) before continuing.

Vocational training centres should not produce outreach messages
The AI tool was incapable of writing outreach messages

Persona assignment only worked for creative writing tasks

Adding as many role assignments as possible to a single prompt
Assuming any professional-sounding role assignment will help
